extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, peer reviewers, methodologists, and clinicians concerned with biomedical reporting quality
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical findings on how to define, measure, and reduce 'spin' (biased or misleading reporting/interpretation) across biomedical study designs, with recommended instruments and assessment procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting practices that distort interpretation and create misleading, favourable conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Reporting practices that distort the interpretation of results and create misleading conclusions, suggesting a more favourable result’ (identified in 20/35 included reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include explicit strategies to highlight treatment benefit despite nonsignificant primary outcomes or reframing results to emphasize favorable findings; used as one of four inductive definition categories of spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discordance between results and their interpretation (overly favourable interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Discordance between results and their interpretation, with the interpretation being more favourable than the results’ (identified in 9/35 included reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized by comparing data presented in results sections with the authors’ conclusions; used as a measurable outcome (e.g., whether abstract conclusion is discordant with study results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of causality when study design does not support it
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Attribution of causality when study design does not allow for it’ (identified in 3/35 included reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly relevant to nonrandomised/observational studies where causal language (e.g., 'X increases Y', 'this shows that') is inappropriate and constitutes spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overinterpretation or inappropriate extrapolation of results
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Overinterpretation or inappropriate extrapolation of results’ (identified in 3/35 included reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes overstating diagnostic accuracy or clinical applicability beyond what data justify; may involve recommending clinical use without sufficient evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement of how often spin occurs (reported by 31/35 reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically reported as percentage of articles containing at least one spin practice; medians and ranges presented by study type and by location (abstract vs main text). Trials (especially with nonsignificant primary outcomes) show highest and most variable prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level or severity of spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the degree or severity of spin in article conclusions (measured in 8–9 reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often operationalized using the Boutron instrument for trials with nonsignificant primary outcomes. Severity/ranking approaches (e.g., Q-sort by experts) have been used to identify the most severe types of spin (e.g., unjustified clinical recommendations, misleading titles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Boutron 'high' level spin (criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boutron et al.'s definition of a ‘high’ level of spin in study conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High spin defined as: no uncertainty in the framing of conclusions, no recommendations for further trials, no acknowledgment of statistically nonsignificant primary outcomes, and/or making recommendations to use the intervention in clinical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practices used to spin results — inappropriate interpretation given study design
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreting nonsignificant results as equivalence or using causal language in observational studies (a common spin practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: treating superiority trials with nonsignificant primary outcomes as showing treatments are 'equally good'; use of causal phrases ('X increases Y') in nonrandomized designs. Identified as the most prevalent practice in nonrandomised study abstracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practices used to spin results — inappropriate extrapolations or clinical recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Making clinical practice recommendations or expressing unwarranted confidence in tests/interventions without supporting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May include recommending clinical use without calling for confirmatory RCTs; in one sample 56% of observational studies endorsed clinical recommendations and 86% of those did not state the need for an RCT.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practices used to spin results — selective reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective emphasis or omission of outcomes to distract from nonsignificant or unfavourable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes omitting nonsignificant endpoints from abstracts/conclusions, focusing on significant secondary outcomes or subgroup analyses, 'cherry picking' significant results, and selective citation of external studies to support interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practices used to spin results — more robust or favourable data presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation tactics that make results appear stronger than warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: overly optimistic abstracts, describing nonsignificance as 'trends', misrepresenting study design as more robust, underreporting adverse events or complications, and rhetorical strategies to make graphical/data representations appear more favourable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prespecified, standardized data collection instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess spin using prespecified or standardized instruments (used by 32/34 reports that assessed published articles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nine reports used or adapted Boutron's instrument; many used author-generated instruments (68%), but only a minority underwent pilot or reliability testing (32%). Validated instruments improve reproducibility across studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive/exploratory instrument development
rubrics_metrics.description: Using inductive methods to identify and classify spin practices rather than only prespecifying them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only 4 reports used inductive methods; inductive approaches capture a broader, potentially more realistic range of spin practices across study designs and should be used to develop generalisable instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment procedures to reduce subjectivity (data extractor methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for assessing spin that reduce interpretive bias in coding (used by majority of reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended practices include multiple independent data extractors, resolving discrepancies via consensus, third-investigator adjudication, and (less commonly) blinding extractors to author/funding/journal. Use of independent coding and adjudication is standard because spin assessment is subjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location of spin assessment (abstract, main text, title)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify where spin is assessed: abstract, main text, and/or title (half of reports assessed both abstract and main text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract spin may have greater practical consequences because clinicians often rely on abstracts alone; some studies assessed only abstracts, some only main texts, and a few assessed titles. Comparisons between locations (e.g., discordant conclusions between abstract and main text) are informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to examine for association with spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess associations between presence of spin and study/journal/author characteristics: conflicts of interest/funding, author characteristics, journal characteristics, study design/quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies were heterogeneous and largely inconclusive; the only consistent positive association was having a nonsignificant primary endpoint. Industry funding was not consistently associated with higher spin (meta-analysis RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.87–1.34).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring effects of spin on readers' interpretation and decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirically assess how spin influences readers' judgments and decisions (rarely measured).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches include randomized experiments (e.g., Boutron RCT showing spin in abstracts led readers to judge treatments as more beneficial and trials as less rigorous) and retrospective comparisons with regulatory reviews (e.g., FDA judgments). More work needed on real-world decision impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards and editorial checks to prevent spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical safeguards recommended for editors, peer reviewers, and guideline developers to minimise spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include checking consistency between abstract and manuscript conclusions, screening for inappropriate causal language and overgeneralisation, developing guidelines based on systematic reviews, promoting open data and independent re-interpretation, and addressing structural incentives in academia that reward 'positive' conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and methodological transparency requirements for spin studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic reporting of spin studies should include definition of spin, location of assessment, methods of measuring spin, instrument development, and inter-rater reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewed authors extracted spin-related findings verbatim and recommended transparent documentation of search strategy, inclusion criteria, instrument validation/piloting, and coding procedures to improve reproducibility and comparability.
